```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# The committed files that the three builds write. The case numbers, strata and
# clusters of the union file are codes, so they are read as text.
trust_ess <- readr::read_csv("../cases/trust/data/trust_ess.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
id_cols <- readr::cols(caseid = readr::col_character(), stratum = readr::col_character(),
                       psu = readr::col_character())
unions <- readr::read_csv("../cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_unions.csv", col_types = id_cols)
months_committed <- readr::read_csv("../cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_months.csv", col_types = id_cols)
panel <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
measures <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/macro/predictor_measures.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
by_edu <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy_edu.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Counts quoted in the text
paper_rows <- datawizard::data_filter(trust_ess, citizen == 1, minority == 0)
window_unions <- datawizard::data_filter(unions, in_window, cycle == "1995" | (cycle == "2006-10" & from_2005))
```

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) is about the work between a download and a model: reading the raw files of a survey, selecting the respondents or the events that a study analyses, recoding the answers into the variables that its paper describes, building the measures that the models need, turning the data into the unit on which the model is fitted, and checking the result against a target that you did not compute yourself. Each of the three-day courses builds the analysis file of its case from the raw files in the second session of day 2, after downloading those files on day 1 by the routes that the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd) sets out, and this module is the reading for that session: [immigration and trust](../tracks/trust-three-days/day-2.qmd), [cohabitation](../tracks/cohabitation-three-days/day-2.qmd) and [EU frames](../tracks/eu-frames-three-days/day-2.qmd). The self-study track takes the EU-frames build in [stage 10](../tracks/self-study/stage-10.qmd), and the one-day data-tools course on the EU-frames case reads its outline in [Part 3](../tracks/eu-frames-one-day-data-tools/part-3.qmd).

Section 1 sets out the steps that every build shares. Sections 2 to 4 take the three cases in turn, each as a sequence of steps with the code that does them: the analysis file of the immigration-and-trust paper from four rounds of the European Social Survey (ESS), the first premarital cohabitations and the person-month file of the cohabitation paper from the union histories of the National Survey of Family Growth (NSFG), and the country-year panel of the EU-frames paper from sixteen Eurobarometer waves. Section 5 draws out the habits that carry over to a project of your own. The module assumes the [R module](intro-r.qmd).

The code of each build is taken from the pipeline of the course, the numbered scripts in `R/<case>/` that write the data files of each case, and from the preparation scripts of the EU-frames workspace, rearranged as a sequence of steps that you can run one at a time in your IDE. Code that reads a raw or licensed file is shown and not run on this page, which is built without those files; what each step produces is shown from the files that the course committed, which the same steps wrote. The cohabitation build below was run on the two NSFG files on 27 October 2026 and reproduced the committed union file, value for value. The immigration-and-trust build was run on the same day on the files from which the extract of the course was made, a cumulative ESS file with the same editions of rounds 1–4 and the Italian country file, and reproduced the committed extract. The second EU-frames script was run on the respondent file on the same day and printed the comparison that section 4.7 quotes. Each build ends with a comparison of your file with the committed one, so that a rebuild on your own machine either reproduces the file of the course or says where it differs.

## 1. The steps of a build {#sec-steps}

Whatever the survey, a build from raw files goes through the same six steps, in this order.

1. **Read** the raw files, with their labels where they have them (Stata and SPSS files carry the wording of each question and answer) or by the column positions that a setup file gives where they have none (fixed-width text).
2. **Select** the rows that the study analyses: its countries, rounds or waves, respondents and events, by the rules that the paper states.
3. **Recode** the answers into the variables that the paper describes: reversed scales, groups, indicators that take the value 0 or 1, dates, and the codes for refusals and non-answers turned into missing values.
4. **Derive** the measures that the models need and that no single question gives: a scale built from several items, the length of a union, the party in government on the day of an interview.
5. **Reshape or aggregate** the rows into the unit on which the model is fitted: one row per respondent, one row per month in which an event could happen, one row per country and year.
6. **Check** the result against a target: the counts of the paper, the file of the course, the checksum of a file.

Three rules hold throughout. The raw files stay in a folder outside the workspace and are never edited; every change is made by the code, so that a reader can see it. The code meets the raw files in one place, a folder named at the top of the script, so that someone else can point the same code at their own copy. And files derived from licensed microdata go into a folder that git ignores, from the first day.

| | Immigration and trust | Cohabitation | EU frames |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raw files | Five ESS files in Stata format | Two NSFG female respondent files in fixed-width text, with their SAS setup files | Sixteen Eurobarometer waves in Stata format |
| Unit of the analysis file | Respondent | Union, then month at risk | Country-year |
| Size | `r format(nrow(trust_ess), big.mark = ",")` respondents, `r format(nrow(paper_rows), big.mark = ",")` in the sample of the paper | `r format(nrow(window_unions), big.mark = ",")` unions in the window of the paper, `r format(nrow(months_committed), big.mark = ",")` months at risk in the wider window | `r nrow(panel)` country-years from `r format(sum(panel$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` respondents |
| Target of the check | The counts of Table 1 of the paper, and the committed extract | The counts of the paper, and the committed union and person-month files | The committed panel, to the precision of floating-point arithmetic |
| Code in the course | `R/trust/01_extract.R` | `R/cohabitation/01_unions.R`, `02_person_months.R` | `prep/01_build_respondents.R` and `prep/02_scales_and_panel.R` in the workspace |
| Who may receive the result | Anyone, under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | Anyone, under the data use restrictions of the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) | The panel, anyone; the respondent file, nobody |

: The three builds at a glance.

## 2. Immigration and trust: the analysis file from the ESS {#sec-trust}

The original author (OA) of the immigration-and-trust case [@McLaren2012CulturalDivideEurope] analysed the respondents of sixteen Western European countries in rounds 1 to 4 of the ESS, keeping those who were citizens of their country and did not belong to an ethnic minority, and built every variable of the model from the questionnaire as the appendix of the paper describes. The extract of the course, `trust_ess.csv`, keeps all `r format(nrow(trust_ess), big.mark = ",")` respondents of the sixteen countries with those variables, so that the sample of the paper is a filter on it. The code below is that of `R/trust/01_extract.R`, which reads a cumulative ESS file held by the course team; here it reads the five Stata files that the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-ess) downloads from the ESS Data Portal. The extract is released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and ships with the workspace, so the build is not needed to run the case: it is the way to learn what each column of the extract is and where it came from.

### 2.1 The files and the variables {#sec-trust-read}

The code needs the folder that holds the five files, the sixteen countries, and the ESS names of the variables that the paper uses. It also needs two lookup tables for the vote controls of section 2.3, which the course built from the crosswalk of Party Facts and the cabinet table of ParlGov (stage 00 of the pipeline) and keeps in `data-raw/trust/` of its repository; the code expects them in the `data/` folder of the workspace. Every party code of the vote questions has a row in the first table, so its column `variable` lists the vote questions to read.

```{r}
#| label: trust-read
#| eval: false
ess_dir <- "../ess_raw"  # the folder that holds the five ESS files

countries <- c("AT", "BE", "CH", "DE", "DK", "ES", "FI", "FR", "GB", "GR", "IE", "IT",
               "NL", "NO", "PT", "SE")
survey_vars <- c("cntry", "essround", "idno", "dweight", "pspwght", "pweight", "ctzcntr", "blgetmg",
                 "trstprl", "trstplt", "trstlgl", "imbgeco", "imueclt", "imwbcnt",
                 "happy", "stflife", "sclmeet", "ppltrst", "pplfair", "pplhlp",
                 "stfeco", "hincfel", "stfhlth", "stfedu", "stfgov", "lrscale",
                 "hinctnt", "hinctnta", "vote", "agea", "gndr", "edulvla",
                 "inwyr", "inwmm", "inwdd", "inwyys", "inwmms", "inwdds")

party_codes <- readr::read_csv("data/party_codes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cabinets <- readr::read_csv("data/cabinets.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
vote_vars <- unique(party_codes$variable)

# Each file is read with only the columns that it holds, its labelled answers
# turned into plain numbers (refusals and non-answers are already missing), and
# the five are stacked into one data frame of the sixteen countries in rounds 1-4
ess <- list.files(ess_dir, pattern = "\\.dta$", full.names = TRUE) |>
  purrr::map(\(f) {
    haven::read_dta(f, col_select = dplyr::any_of(c(survey_vars, vote_vars))) |>
      dplyr::mutate(cntry = as.character(haven::zap_labels(cntry)),
                    dplyr::across(-cntry, \(x) as.numeric(haven::zap_labels(x))))
  }) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  datawizard::data_filter(essround <= 4, cntry %in% countries)
```

Each round asks the same questions under the same names, which is what makes the stacking possible, but not every round asks every question. The interview date has one set of names in rounds 1 and 2 and another in rounds 3 and 4, household income is asked in twelve bands in rounds 1 to 3 and in deciles in round 4, and every country and round has its own question on the party voted for. `dplyr::any_of()` reads whichever of the listed columns are in a file, and `dplyr::bind_rows()` leaves a column empty for the rounds that lack it. The result holds `r format(nrow(trust_ess), big.mark = ",")` respondents in `r nrow(dplyr::distinct(trust_ess, cntry, essround))` country-rounds: Austria has no round 4 in these editions, Greece no round 3 and Italy only rounds 1 and 2, the second of them from the Italian country file.

### 2.2 The date of the interview {#sec-trust-date}

The vote controls depend on the day of the interview, because a respondent who voted for a party counts as a voter for a governing party only if that party sat in the cabinet on that day. Rounds 1 and 2 record the date of the interview and rounds 3 and 4 the date on which it started. A date that is missing, or that falls outside the years in which the four rounds were fielded, takes the middle date of its country-round, so that the cabinet in office can still be read.

```{r}
#| label: trust-date
#| eval: false
ess <- ess |>
  dplyr::mutate(date = lubridate::make_date(dplyr::coalesce(inwyys, inwyr), dplyr::coalesce(inwmms, inwmm),
                                            dplyr::coalesce(inwdds, inwdd)),
                date = dplyr::if_else(dplyr::between(date, as.Date("2002-01-01"), as.Date("2010-12-31")),
                                      date, NA)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(date = dplyr::coalesce(date, stats::median(date, na.rm = TRUE)), .by = c(cntry, essround))
```

### 2.3 The vote controls {#sec-trust-votes}

The paper controls for two things about the vote at the last national election: whether the respondent voted for a party that was in government at the time of the survey, which it calls being a winner, and whether the respondent voted for a far-right party of the list in its web appendix. The ESS asks the vote question with one list of parties for each country and round, and two votes in Germany, for the constituency and the list. The build turns the vote columns into one row per vote (`datawizard::data_to_long()`), attaches to each party code its keys in ParlGov and its far-right flag, attaches to each vote the cabinet that was in office on the day of the interview, and then collapses the rows back to one per respondent. The cabinet in office is the one whose start date is the last before the interview, which `dplyr::join_by()` expresses as the closest start date that is not later than the interview.

```{r}
#| label: trust-votes
#| eval: false
held_votes <- intersect(vote_vars, names(ess))
votes <- ess |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("cntry", "essround", "idno", "date", held_votes)) |>
  datawizard::data_to_long(select = held_votes, names_to = "variable", values_to = "code",
                           values_drop_na = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(party_codes, by = c("cntry", "essround", "variable", "code"))

# One row per cabinet, with the ParlGov keys of its parties as a list
in_office <- cabinets |>
  dplyr::summarise(cabinet_ids = list(parlgov_id), .by = c(cntry, cabinet, start_date))

# A respondent votes for the cabinet, or for the far right, when either German vote does
vote_flags <- votes |>
  dplyr::left_join(in_office, by = dplyr::join_by(cntry, closest(date >= start_date))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(in_cabinet = purrr::map2_lgl(parlgov_id, cabinet_ids, \(ids, cab) {
    !is.na(ids) && any(as.integer(stringr::str_split_1(ids, ";")) %in% cab)
  })) |>
  dplyr::summarise(winner = as.integer(any(in_cabinet)), far_right_vote = as.integer(any(far_right == 1)),
                   .by = c(cntry, essround, idno))
```

A party code can carry more than one ParlGov key, separated by a semicolon, when the ESS lists an electoral alliance as one party, so the code splits the keys and asks whether any of them sat in the cabinet. Among the `r format(nrow(paper_rows), big.mark = ",")` respondents of the paper, `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(paper_rows$voted, na.rm = TRUE))` voted at the last national election, `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(paper_rows$winner))` voted for a party in the cabinet on the day of their interview, and `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(paper_rows$far_right_vote))` for a far-right party of the appendix. Neither control can be rebuilt from the paper alone. The paper names no cabinets, and its web appendix lists the far-right parties by name rather than by their codes in the ESS, so every rebuild has to make the links itself, and the [case study](../cases/trust/index.qmd#sec-course-rebuild) shows that the whole gap between the extract of the course and the first SCORE reproduction lies in these two variables.

### 2.4 Income and the reversed scales {#sec-trust-recode}

The last step joins the vote controls to the respondents and writes every variable in the form that the appendix of the paper describes. The trust items and the immigration items are reversed (10 minus the answer), so that a high value means more distrust and more concern about immigration, and so are the controls of the same kind. Household income is standardised within each country-round, because the bands of rounds 1 to 3 and the deciles of round 4 cannot be compared directly; `datawizard::standardize()` subtracts the mean of the country-round and divides by its standard deviation. A respondent who gave no vote, or no party, counts as 0 on both vote controls.

```{r}
#| label: trust-extract
#| eval: false
trust_ess <- ess |>
  dplyr::left_join(vote_flags, by = c("cntry", "essround", "idno")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(hh_income = dplyr::coalesce(hinctnt, hinctnta)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(hh_income_z = as.numeric(datawizard::standardize(hh_income)), .by = c(cntry, essround)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    cntry, essround, idno,
    citizen = as.integer(ctzcntr == 1), minority = as.integer(blgetmg == 1),
    dweight = round(dweight, 4), pspwght = round(pspwght, 4), pweight = signif(pweight, 5),
    distrust_parl = 10 - trstprl, distrust_pol = 10 - trstplt, distrust_legal = 10 - trstlgl,
    imm_econ = 10 - imbgeco, imm_culture = 10 - imueclt, imm_place = 10 - imwbcnt,
    unhappy = 10 - happy, life_dissat = 10 - stflife, meet_rarely = 8 - sclmeet,
    distrust_people = 10 - ppltrst, unfair_people = 10 - pplfair, unhelpful_people = 10 - pplhlp,
    econ_dissat = 10 - stfeco, income_difficulty = hincfel,
    health_dissat = 10 - stfhlth, educ_dissat = 10 - stfedu, gov_dissat = 10 - stfgov,
    left_right = lrscale, hh_income_z = round(hh_income_z, 3),
    voted = dplyr::case_when(vote == 1 ~ 1L, vote %in% 2:3 ~ 0L),
    winner = dplyr::coalesce(winner, 0L), far_right_vote = dplyr::coalesce(far_right_vote, 0L),
    age = agea, female = as.integer(gndr == 2),
    education = dplyr::if_else(edulvla %in% 1:5, edulvla, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange(c("cntry", "essround", "idno"))
```

Every column of the result is described in the [codebook of the extract](../cases/trust/data/trust_ess_codebook.md), with the ESS variable from which it was built. The means of the reversed trust items among the respondents of the paper come out close to those of Table 1 of the paper: `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(paper_rows$distrust_parl, na.rm = TRUE))` for parliament, `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(paper_rows$distrust_pol, na.rm = TRUE))` for politicians and `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(paper_rows$distrust_legal, na.rm = TRUE))` for the legal system, against 5.07, 6.05 and 4.46 in the paper.

### 2.5 The check {#sec-trust-check}

The paper gives two counts against which the build can be checked: 120,080 respondents in all (its note 40), and the respondents of its sample by country (Table 1), whose total is 110,732. The second check compares the file that you built with the extract that the workspace ships, column by column and value by value, with `all.equal()`, which allows for the rounding of floating-point arithmetic.

```{r}
#| label: trust-check
#| eval: false
table1 <- c(AT = 6310, BE = 6648, CH = 6551, DE = 10719, DK = 5843, ES = 7189, FI = 7946,
            FR = 6835, GB = 7905, GR = 6249, IE = 7187, IT = 2698, NL = 7344, NO = 6653,
            PT = 7406, SE = 7249)
paper_n <- trust_ess |>
  datawizard::data_filter(citizen == 1, minority == 0) |>
  dplyr::count(cntry)
stopifnot(nrow(trust_ess) == 120080, all(paper_n$n == table1[paper_n$cntry]))

# The shipped extract leaves out the respondent number
committed <- readr::read_csv("data/trust_ess.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
rebuilt <- datawizard::data_select(trust_ess, exclude = "idno")
identical(names(committed), names(rebuilt))
all.equal(committed, rebuilt, check.attributes = FALSE)
```

Both return `TRUE` when the five files are the editions listed in the data sources module. A comparison of values is safer here than a comparison of checksums. An MD5 sum is computed from the bytes of a file, and git on Windows, unless it is told otherwise, writes the end of every line of a text file as two characters rather than one, which changes the sum of a CSV file without changing a single value in it. The count by country is the same in the extract and in the paper for all sixteen countries:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trust-table1
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Respondents of the paper (citizens who do not belong to an ethnic minority) by country, as the paper counts them and in the extract of the course. Sources: the table of descriptive statistics of the paper (its Table 1) and `cases/trust/data/trust_ess.csv`."
extract_counts <- dplyr::count(paper_rows, cntry, name = "extract")
tibble::tribble(
  ~cntry, ~paper,
  "AT", 6310, "BE", 6648, "CH", 6551, "DE", 10719, "DK", 5843, "ES", 7189, "FI", 7946, "FR", 6835,
  "GB", 7905, "GR", 6249, "IE", 7187, "IT", 2698, "NL", 7344, "NO", 6653, "PT", 7406, "SE", 7249
) |>
  dplyr::left_join(extract_counts, by = "cntry") |>
  datawizard::data_rename(select = c(Country = "cntry", Paper = "paper", Extract = "extract")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::format_tt(j = 2:3, digits = 0, num_fmt = "decimal", num_mark_big = ",")
```

### 2.6 The analysis file of the paper {#sec-trust-analysis}

The extract is not yet the file on which a model is fitted. Three more steps make it so, and they run from the committed extract, so this page runs them: keep the respondents of the paper, build the two scales that the paper uses from their items, and keep the rows that answered everything that the model needs. The paper averages the three immigration items into one index of concern, and the three items on other people into an index of interpersonal distrust. `datawizard::row_means()` averages the items of each row; with `min_valid = 3` an index is missing unless all three items were answered.

```{r}
#| label: trust-analysis
analysis <- trust_ess |>
  datawizard::data_filter(citizen == 1, minority == 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    concern_idx = datawizard::row_means(dplyr::pick(imm_econ, imm_culture, imm_place), min_valid = 3),
    soc_distrust_idx = datawizard::row_means(dplyr::pick(distrust_people, unfair_people, unhelpful_people),
                                             min_valid = 3)
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("cntry", "essround", "distrust_parl", "concern_idx", "age", "female", "education",
                            "hh_income_z", "unhappy", "life_dissat", "meet_rarely", "soc_distrust_idx",
                            "left_right", "econ_dissat", "income_difficulty", "health_dissat",
                            "educ_dissat", "winner", "far_right_vote")) |>
  tidyr::drop_na()

c(respondents = nrow(analysis), country_rounds = nrow(dplyr::distinct(analysis, cntry, essround)))
```

The paper reports `r format(nrow(paper_rows), big.mark = ",")` respondents in every model, yet household income is missing for `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(is.na(paper_rows$hh_income_z)))` of them, and dropping every row with a missing answer leaves the `r format(nrow(analysis), big.mark = ",")` above, in `r nrow(dplyr::distinct(analysis, cntry, essround))` of the 60 country-rounds. The paper does not say how it treated the missing answers, and both SCORE reproductions analysed about this many respondents. The course keeps this file as its reference, and the [specification menu](../cases/trust/menu.qmd) offers the other rule for the scales, averaging whichever items were answered, as one of its decisions.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Change `min_valid = 3` to `min_valid = 1` for both indices, so that each is the mean of the items that were answered, and run the chunk again. How many respondents does the analysis file gain? Then leave out `hh_income_z` and count again, and write one sentence on which of the two decisions costs the paper more of its sample.
:::

## 3. Cohabitation: unions and person-months from the NSFG {#sec-cohabitation}

The original authors (OAs) of the cohabitation case [@KuoRaley2016DivergingPatternsUnion] compared the first premarital cohabitations of American women begun in 1990–1995, from the NSFG of 1995, with those begun in 2005–2010, from the NSFG of 2006–2010, keeping unions that began no more than five years before the interview and lasted at least a month, and fitted their models to person-month data: "the first month indicating the month when cohabitation started and last month the month when cohabitation was ended either by marriage or separation or the month when interview was conducted for those whose first premarital cohabitation remained intact at the time of interview (i.e., censoring)". The course rebuilt those unions from the public-use files. `R/cohabitation/01_unions.R` reads five surveys of the NSFG, the two of the paper and three later ones; the steps below read the two of the paper, and the others are read in the same way as 2006–2010. The union file and the person-month file are committed, in the public domain under the data use restrictions of NCHS, and the union file ships with the workspace of the case. The [case study](../cases/cohabitation/index.qmd#sec-data) describes the unions of the paper.

### 3.1 Column positions from the setup files {#sec-cohab-positions}

A fixed-width file has no column names and no separators, so the first step reads the positions of the variables from the INPUT statement of each SAS setup file, as the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-nsfg) shows it: a name, an optional `$` for a text variable, and a column or a range of columns. A regular expression picks the name and the columns out of the text, and the result is one row per variable with its first and last column.

```{r}
#| label: cohab-positions
#| eval: false
nsfg_dir <- "../nsfg_raw"  # the folder that holds the NSFG files

positions <- c(`1995` = "sas/1995FemRespSetup.sas", `2006-10` = "sas/2006_2010_FemRespSetup.sas") |>
  purrr::map(\(f) {
    lines <- readr::read_lines(file.path(nsfg_dir, f))
    first <- stringr::str_which(lines, stringr::regex("^\\s*input\\s*$|^\\s*input\\s", ignore_case = TRUE))[1]
    last <- first + stringr::str_which(lines[first:length(lines)], ";")[1] - 1
    paste(lines[first:last], collapse = " ") |>
      stringr::str_match_all("([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)\\s+(?:\\$\\s*)?(\\d+)(?:\\s*-\\s*(\\d+))?") |>
      purrr::pluck(1) |>
      tibble::as_tibble(.name_repair = \(x) c("match", "name", "begin", "end")) |>
      dplyr::transmute(name = toupper(name), begin = as.integer(begin),
                       end = dplyr::coalesce(as.integer(end), as.integer(begin))) |>
      datawizard::data_filter(name != "INPUT") |>
      dplyr::distinct(name, .keep_all = TRUE)
  })
```

### 3.2 The two surveys {#sec-cohab-read}

Each file is read with only the variables that the build needs, as text first, because some fields hold a full stop for a missing value, and then as numbers. The 1995 survey has no recode for the length of the first cohabitation, so it needs the dates of the marriages and of the cohabitations with former partners, from which the end of the union is found in section 3.3; from 2002 the recodes give the length directly. The names of the weight and of the design variables, the strata and the clusters that the errors of every model of the case take into account, differ between the two surveys.

```{r}
#| label: cohab-read
#| eval: false
vars_1995 <- c("CASEID", "BDAYCENM", "A_DOI", "AGE", "FMARNO", paste0("MARDAT0", 1:5), "HIEDUC", "HISPRACE",
               "COHAB1", "COHSTAT", "COHOUT", "COHAB1_I", "COHOUT_I", paste0("STRTOGH", 1:4), "STRTOGCH",
               paste0("STRTOTH", 0:7), paste0("STOPOTH", 0:7), "POST_WT", "COL_STR", "PANEL")
vars_0610 <- c("CASEID", "CMBIRTH", "CMINTVW", "AGER", "HIEDUC", "HISPRACE", "COHAB1", "COHSTAT", "COHOUT",
               "COH1DUR", "COHAB1_I", "COHOUT_I", "COH1DUR_I", "HAVEDEG", "DIPGED", "EDUCAT", "QUESTYEAR",
               "WGTQ1Q16", "SEST", "SECU")

pos_1995 <- datawizard::data_filter(positions[["1995"]], name %in% vars_1995)
pos_0610 <- datawizard::data_filter(positions[["2006-10"]], name %in% vars_0610)
stopifnot(setequal(pos_1995$name, vars_1995), setequal(pos_0610$name, vars_0610))

raw_1995 <- readr::read_fwf(file.path(nsfg_dir, "1995FemRespData.dat"),
                            readr::fwf_positions(pos_1995$begin, pos_1995$end, pos_1995$name),
                            col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character())) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(),
                              \(v) readr::parse_number(stringr::str_trim(v), na = c("", "."))))
raw_0610 <- readr::read_fwf(file.path(nsfg_dir, "2006_2010_FemResp.dat"),
                            readr::fwf_positions(pos_0610$begin, pos_0610$end, pos_0610$name),
                            col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character())) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(),
                              \(v) readr::parse_number(stringr::str_trim(v), na = c("", "."))))
```

The 1995 file holds 10,847 women and the 2006–2010 file 12,279, the counts that the paper gives, and `nrow()` of each data frame is the first check that the file was read whole.

### 3.3 Dates and the end of a union {#sec-cohab-end}

The NSFG records dates as **century months**, the number of months since December 1899, so that January 1900 is 1 and January 2005 is 1261; the length of an interval in months is a subtraction. Values from 9997 up are the codes for a date that was not ascertained, refused or not known, and they become missing values.

From 2002 the end of the first cohabitation is its start plus its length, the recode `COH1DUR`, which counts the months to the interview for an intact union, to the marriage for one that became a marriage, and to the end of living together for one that dissolved. The 2006–2010 file also needs a correction. NCHS found that from the second year of interviewing some women with a GED and twelve or fewer years of school had been given their years of school on `HIEDUC` rather than the code of a high school diploma, and published the rule that corrects it, which the code applies as `hieduc_fixed`.

```{r}
#| label: cohab-0610
#| eval: false
women_0610 <- raw_0610 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    hieduc_fixed = dplyr::if_else(HAVEDEG %in% c(NA, 5) & DIPGED %in% 2 & dplyr::between(EDUCAT, 9, 12) &
                                    QUESTYEAR >= 2, 9, HIEDUC),
    dplyr::across(c(CMBIRTH, CMINTVW, COHAB1), \(v) dplyr::if_else(v >= 9997, NA_real_, v))
  ) |>
  dplyr::transmute(cycle = "2006-10", caseid = as.character(CASEID), cm_birth = CMBIRTH,
                   cm_interview = CMINTVW, age_interview = AGER, cohstat = COHSTAT, cohout = COHOUT,
                   cm_start = COHAB1, cm_end = cm_start + COH1DUR,
                   imputed = COHAB1_I %in% 1 | COHOUT_I %in% 1 | COH1DUR_I %in% 1,
                   hieduc = HIEDUC, hieduc_fixed, hisprace = HISPRACE,
                   weight = WGTQ1Q16, stratum = SEST, psu = SECU)
```

The 1995 file gives the start of the first cohabitation (`COHAB1`) and its outcome (`COHOUT`: intact, a marriage that lasted, a marriage that dissolved, or a dissolved cohabitation), but not its end. The recode specification of the survey (pages 262–263 of the user guide of Cycle 5) builds `COHAB1` from the dates on which the woman began to live with each husband and with each partner whom she did not marry, so the end of the union comes from the same source. For a union that became a marriage it is the date of the marriage to the husband with whom it began; for a union that dissolved it is the date on which the woman stopped living with that partner, "the last time"; for an intact union it is the interview. The code finds each by matching the start dates of the husbands and of the former partners with `COHAB1`, after turning the questions on husbands and partners into one row per husband or partner (`tidyr::pivot_longer()`).

```{r}
#| label: cohab-1995
#| eval: false
husband_start <- c(STRTOGH1 = "MARDAT01", STRTOGH2 = "MARDAT02", STRTOGH3 = "MARDAT03", STRTOGH4 = "MARDAT04")
date_vars <- c("BDAYCENM", "A_DOI", paste0("MARDAT0", 1:5), names(husband_start), "STRTOGCH",
               paste0("STRTOTH", 0:7), paste0("STOPOTH", 0:7))
raw_1995 <- dplyr::mutate(raw_1995, dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(date_vars),
                                                  \(v) dplyr::if_else(v >= 9997, NA_real_, v)))

# The marriage date of the husband with whom the first cohabitation began; the
# current husband (STRTOGCH) is the most recent marriage
marriage_dates <- raw_1995 |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("CASEID", paste0("MARDAT0", 1:5))) |>
  datawizard::data_to_long(select = paste0("MARDAT0", 1:5), names_to = "mardat", values_to = "end_marriage")
marriage_end <- raw_1995 |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("CASEID", "COHAB1", "FMARNO", names(husband_start), "STRTOGCH")) |>
  datawizard::data_to_long(select = c(names(husband_start), "STRTOGCH"), names_to = "source",
                           values_to = "cm_together") |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(cm_together), cm_together == COHAB1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(mardat = dplyr::if_else(source == "STRTOGCH", paste0("MARDAT0", pmin(FMARNO, 5)),
                                        husband_start[source])) |>
  dplyr::left_join(marriage_dates, by = c("CASEID", "mardat")) |>
  dplyr::arrange(CASEID, source) |>
  dplyr::summarise(end_marriage = dplyr::first(end_marriage), .by = CASEID)

# The date on which the woman stopped living with the first former partner
# whose start date is COHAB1
dissolution_end <- raw_1995 |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("CASEID", "COHAB1", paste0("STRTOTH", 0:7), paste0("STOPOTH", 0:7))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-c(CASEID, COHAB1), names_to = c(".value", "partner"),
                      names_pattern = "(STRTOTH|STOPOTH)(\\d)") |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(STRTOTH), STRTOTH == COHAB1) |>
  dplyr::arrange(CASEID, partner) |>
  dplyr::summarise(end_dissolution = dplyr::first(STOPOTH), .by = CASEID)

women_1995 <- raw_1995 |>
  dplyr::left_join(marriage_end, by = "CASEID") |>
  dplyr::left_join(dissolution_end, by = "CASEID") |>
  dplyr::transmute(cycle = "1995", caseid = as.character(CASEID), cm_birth = BDAYCENM,
                   cm_interview = A_DOI, age_interview = AGE, cohstat = COHSTAT, cohout = COHOUT,
                   cm_start = COHAB1,
                   cm_end = dplyr::case_when(COHOUT == 1 ~ A_DOI,
                                             COHOUT %in% 2:3 ~ dplyr::coalesce(end_marriage, MARDAT01),
                                             COHOUT == 4 ~ end_dissolution),
                   imputed = COHAB1_I %in% 1 | COHOUT_I %in% 1,
                   hieduc = HIEDUC, hieduc_fixed = HIEDUC, hisprace = HISPRACE,
                   weight = POST_WT, stratum = COL_STR, psu = PANEL)
```

Fourteen of the 1995 unions that dissolved have no stop date (it was not ascertained, refused or not known), and one ends before it begins. Ten of the fourteen began more than five years before the interview, so the window of the paper would leave them out anyway; the other four began within it but have no length, so they cannot be shown to have lasted a month, and the window leaves them out as well.

### 3.4 The unions and their measures {#sec-cohab-unions}

The two surveys are stacked, and the build keeps the women whose first cohabitation came before any marriage (`COHSTAT` = 2, a recode that every survey carries) and derives what the models need: the outcome in three categories, the length of the union and the time from its start to the interview in months, the calendar year and the age of the woman at its start, education in the four groups of the paper, race and Hispanic origin, and the two flags of the window of the paper. Education is coded twice, as the paper codes it, with the associate degree counted as some college and the corrected `HIEDUC`, and as the person-month file of SCORE codes it, with the associate degree counted as college and `HIEDUC` as released, because the [specification menu](../cases/cohabitation/menu.qmd) offers both. The strata and clusters are prefixed with the survey, so that the codes of two surveys can never be mistaken for one another.

```{r}
#| label: cohab-unions
#| eval: false
unions <- dplyr::bind_rows(women_1995, women_0610) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(cohstat == 2) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    outcome = dplyr::case_when(cohout == 1 ~ "intact", cohout %in% 2:3 ~ "marriage", cohout == 4 ~ "separation"),
    duration = cm_end - cm_start,
    since_start = cm_interview - cm_start,
    year_start = 1900 + (cm_start - 1) %/% 12,
    age_start = (cm_start - cm_birth) / 12,
    educ = dplyr::case_when(hieduc_fixed <= 8 ~ "less_hs", hieduc_fixed == 9 ~ "hs",
                            hieduc_fixed %in% 10:11 ~ "some_college", hieduc_fixed >= 12 ~ "college"),
    educ_score = dplyr::case_when(hieduc <= 8 ~ "less_hs", hieduc == 9 ~ "hs", hieduc == 10 ~ "some_college",
                                  hieduc >= 11 ~ "college"),
    race = dplyr::case_when(hisprace == 1 ~ "hispanic", hisprace == 2 ~ "white", hisprace == 3 ~ "black",
                            hisprace == 4 ~ "other"),
    in_window = since_start <= 60 & duration >= 1,  # begun within five years, lasted a month or more
    from_2005 = cm_start >= (2005 - 1900) * 12 + 1,  # begun in January 2005 or later
    stratum = paste(cycle, stratum, sep = "_"),
    psu = paste(stratum, psu, sep = "_")
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("cycle", "caseid", "weight", "stratum", "psu", "cm_interview", "cm_start", "cm_end",
                            "year_start", "since_start", "duration", "outcome", "age_start", "age_interview",
                            "educ", "educ_score", "race", "hieduc", "hieduc_fixed", "hisprace", "imputed",
                            "in_window", "from_2005")) |>
  dplyr::arrange(cycle, caseid)
```

### 3.5 The check {#sec-cohab-check}

The paper gives the counts of its unions and their outcomes: 929 unions begun between 1990 and 1995, of which "340 marriages occurred, 347 cohabitors broke up, and 242 stayed together at the time of interview", and 1,142 begun between 2005 and 2010, with 194, 504 and 444. The window of the paper keeps the unions with `in_window`, and in 2006–2010 only those with `from_2005`. In the committed union file:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cohab-counts
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "First premarital cohabitations in the window of the paper, by survey and outcome. Source: `cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_unions.csv`; the paper gives 340, 347 and 242 for 1995 and 194, 504 and 444 for 2006–2010."
window_unions |>
  dplyr::count(cycle, outcome) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = n) |>
  dplyr::mutate(unions = marriage + separation + intact) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c(Survey = "cycle", Unions = "unions", Marriage = "marriage",
                            Separation = "separation", Intact = "intact")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::format_tt(j = 2:5, digits = 0, num_fmt = "decimal", num_mark_big = ",")
```

Your rebuild of the two surveys should equal the rows of the committed file for those surveys, with the same columns in the same order and the same values, which `all.equal()` checks with the tolerance of floating-point arithmetic:

```{r}
#| label: cohab-check
#| eval: false
committed <- readr::read_csv("data/cohab_unions.csv",
                             col_types = readr::cols(caseid = readr::col_character(),
                                                     stratum = readr::col_character(),
                                                     psu = readr::col_character())) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(cycle %in% c("1995", "2006-10"))
identical(names(committed), names(unions))
all.equal(committed, unions, check.attributes = FALSE)
```

Both return `TRUE`. The weighted shares of the cohabitors by race and Hispanic origin reproduce those of Table 1 of the paper to two decimals, and so do the shares by education, but only with the coding of education that the paper uses (section 3.4), as the [codebook of the union file](../cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_unions_codebook.md) records.

### 3.6 Person-months {#sec-person-months}

A union observed for six months and one observed for five years cannot be compared by whether they had married by the interview, because the first had less time in which to do so. The models of the paper are therefore fitted to **person-month** data, one row for every month in which the union could have ended, with the outcome recorded in the last row; the [event-history module](event-history.qmd) explains why. `survival::survSplit()` does the expansion: it cuts each union at every month and keeps its outcome in its last row only. A union is at risk from the month in which the couple moved in (month 1) to the month of the marriage, the separation or the interview, `duration + 1` months in all. This step runs from the committed union file, so this page runs it, for both surveys in the wider window that the specification menu offers (every union begun within five years of the interview, with `from_2005` marking those that the paper keeps):

```{r}
#| label: cohab-months
at_risk <- unions |>
  datawizard::data_filter(cycle %in% c("1995", "2006-10"), since_start <= 60, !is.na(duration), duration >= 1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(later = as.integer(cycle == "2006-10"),
                month = duration + 1,
                status = factor(outcome, levels = c("intact", "marriage", "separation")))

# survSplit() names the first level of the status, the censoring, "censor", so
# the outcome is read back from the position of the level
months <- survival::survSplit(at_risk, cut = seq_len(max(at_risk$month) - 1), end = "month",
                              event = "status", start = "month_start") |>
  dplyr::mutate(y = c("intact", "marriage", "separation")[as.integer(status)],
                year_of_union = pmin(ceiling(month / 12), 5),
                age_start = round(age_start, 3)) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("cycle", "caseid", "month", "year_of_union", "y", "later", "from_2005",
                            "age_start", "race", "educ", "weight", "stratum", "psu"))

tibble::tibble(unions = nrow(at_risk), person_months = nrow(months),
               same_as_committed = identical(names(months), names(months_committed)) &&
                 isTRUE(all.equal(months, months_committed, check.attributes = FALSE)))
```

The `r format(nrow(at_risk), big.mark = ",")` unions become `r format(nrow(months), big.mark = ",")` rows, the same as `cohab_months.csv`. A union that began in a month and ended in marriage two months later contributes three rows, two `intact` and the last `marriage`:

```{r}
#| label: cohab-one-union
example <- at_risk |>
  datawizard::data_filter(duration == 2, outcome == "marriage") |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 1)
months |>
  dplyr::semi_join(example, by = c("cycle", "caseid")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("cycle", "month", "year_of_union", "y", "later"))
```

The window of the paper, the unions of 1995 and those of 2006–2010 that began in 2005 or later, holds `r format(sum(months$cycle == "1995" | months$from_2005), big.mark = ",")` of these person-months, from `r format(nrow(window_unions), big.mark = ",")` unions. The paper reports 54,291 person-months for the same unions (Table 2), a count that no construction tried by the course reproduces, although the coefficients of Table 2 are reproduced closely; the [codebook of the person-month file](../cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_months_codebook.md) lists the constructions that were tried. The models of the course start from the union file rather than from this one, because a specification can change which unions and which months enter: a three-year horizon, for one, stops every union at month 36.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Build the person-months of a three-year horizon: set `month` to `pmin(duration + 1, 36)` and the status of every union that lasted beyond 36 months to `intact` before calling `survival::survSplit()`. How many rows are left, and how many marriages and separations among them? Compare the share of months that end in a marriage in the two surveys, and say why it is a hazard rather than a share of unions.
:::

## 4. EU frames: the country-year panel from the Eurobarometer {#sec-eu-frames}

The original author (OA) of the EU-frames case [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic] scored the answers of the respondents of sixteen Eurobarometer waves to the question on what the European Union means to them into four framing scales, and modelled them within their countries and waves, with two economic series merged by country and year. The course panel, `EUframes_cy.csv`, averages the same respondents into 270 country-years, as analyst C6HJR did in Multi100, and every page of the one-day courses starts from it. The three-day course builds it from the raw waves with two scripts of the workspace: `prep/01_build_respondents.R`, which you run once, and `prep/02_scales_and_panel.R`, which you read and run step by step. The first rebuilds the respondent file of the course from your own GESIS downloads and checks the result against the course build. The second rebuilds the country-year panel that is distributed with the course, to machine precision, and then builds the panel by education band on which the individual-level extension is based. The pipeline of the case does the same work for the curve of the claim in `R/eu-frames/01_person_file.R` and `07_measurement_panels.R`, and `15_analyst_panels.R` builds, from the same waves, the panels of two of the five analysts, following the code that each deposited.

If you have not downloaded the sixteen files, everything here can still be read, because what the scripts print is quoted on the page; nothing that reads the respondent file can be run.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Licensed microdata {#the-file-you-are-about-to-build-is-licensed-microdata}

The GESIS terms of use apply to everything that the first script writes. The respondent file stays in `data_private/`, which is kept out of version control by the `.gitignore` file in the workspace. It is never uploaded, shared, or opened in a session that an AI assistant can read, because the terms prohibit processing the data with AI systems. It is deleted when the project ends. The aggregates distributed with the course are subject to none of these restrictions, and the second script shows where the line between the two falls.
:::

### 4.1 The respondent file {#sec-build}

`prep/01_build_respondents.R` is written to be run as a whole: set the folder that holds the sixteen files at the top, then source the script. It does five things, and it prints a report at the end.

**It checks the files.** The script contains an inventory of the sixteen studies: the file name under which GESIS serves each study, the study number, the wave, the year to which the course assigns the wave, where the battery of the question starts, the column of the design weight, and the MD5 checksum of the file from which the course panel was built. The first rows read:

```{r}
#| label: eu-inventory
#| eval: false
inventory <- tibble::tribble(
  ~file,               ~study,   ~eb,    ~year, ~cntry_v,   ~items_from, ~items_style, ~w1_v, ~md5,
  "ZA4056_v1-0-1.dta", "ZA4056", "61.0", 2004, "isocntry",  63,  "v",    "v9", "0fc7763a1b0ae4bac6fb70bf87d07543",
  "ZA4229_v1-1-0.dta", "ZA4229", "62.0", 2004, "v7",        105, "v",    "v8", "76051b80553ee29be104d13777eeae31",
  "ZA5689_v2-0-0.dta", "ZA5689", "79.3", 2013, "isocntry",  0,   "qa14", "w1", "e46f479d0d82b4d0cc3fccd69b708397"
)
```

A missing file stops the script with the study number to fetch. The two studies that GESIS serves zipped, ZA4506 and ZA4744, are unpacked beside their archives. The checksum of every file is compared with the inventory, and the report says, file by file, whether yours is byte for byte identical to the one that the course used. The comparison makes the rest of the course reproducible on your own machine. If the sixteen checksums match, every number on this site can be rebuilt from your folder.

**It finds the question in each file.** The battery on what the EU means occupies sixteen adjacent columns in every file, fourteen items followed by "other" and "don't know", but the position of those columns differs. In the twelve older files the columns are numbered (`v63` to `v78` in EB 61.0, `v105` onwards in EB 62.0) and in the four newest they are named after the question (`qa12_1` to `qa12_16` in EB 76.3). The inventory records the start of the block or the question stem for each wave, and the script reads the sixteen columns by that rule and checks that every value is 0 or 1. The respondent characteristics are found differently, by their variable labels rather than their positions, because the occupation item in particular moves from wave to wave. If a label pattern matches two variables, the script stops instead of picking one.

**It harmonises Germany and the United Kingdom**, which the survey samples as two regions each, into one country each, and keeps the twenty-seven member states of the period.

**It codes the respondent characteristics as the published models code them.** Sex as a female indicator. Education as the age at which full-time schooling finished, with the two codings that the [individual-level exercise](individual-level.qmd) offers: the published three bands, which replace "still studying" with the current age of the respondent and cut at 16 and 20, and a four-band version that keeps the students as a band of their own. Occupation collapsed into the eight groups of the published models, with the unemployed as their own group. Urbanisation in three categories. Left–right placement on its ten-point scale, missing in the four waves that did not ask it. The step is one call of `dplyr::mutate()` on the stacked waves:

```{r}
#| label: eu-characteristics
#| eval: false
respondents <- respondents |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    female  = as.integer(gender == 2),
    edu_raw = edu,
    edu4    = dplyr::case_when(edu_raw == 98            ~ "studying",
                               edu_raw %in% c(97, 0:15) ~ "le15",
                               edu_raw %in% 16:19       ~ "e16_19",
                               edu_raw %in% 20:96       ~ "e20plus",
                               TRUE                     ~ NA_character_),
    edu     = dplyr::if_else(edu %in% c(0, 97, 99), NA_real_, edu),
    edu     = dplyr::if_else(edu == 98, age, edu),
    edu3    = dplyr::case_when(edu < 16              ~ "low",
                               edu >= 16 & edu <= 19 ~ "mid",
                               edu > 19              ~ "high",
                               TRUE                  ~ NA_character_),
    ses     = dplyr::case_when(occ %in% 5:9   ~ "self_employed",
                               occ %in% 10:12 ~ "manager",
                               occ %in% 13:14 ~ "white_collar",
                               occ %in% 15:18 ~ "manual",
                               occ == 1       ~ "house_person",
                               occ == 3       ~ "unemployed",
                               occ == 4       ~ "retired",
                               occ == 2       ~ "student",
                               TRUE           ~ NA_character_),
    unemployed = as.integer(ses == "unemployed"),
    urban   = dplyr::case_when(urban == 1 ~ "rural", urban == 2 ~ "small_town",
                               urban == 3 ~ "large_town", TRUE ~ NA_character_),
    rile    = dplyr::if_else(rile %in% 1:10, rile, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(exclude = c("gender", "occ"))
```

**It compares the result with the course files.** The number of respondents in every country-year is checked against the committed panel, and the counts of respondents who named none of the thirteen items, split into those who said "don't know", those who gave another answer and those who left the question blank, are checked against the committed cell file. When the checksums match, all 270 cells match on both counts. On a folder holding the sixteen files that the course used, the printed report looks like this:

```
 study  eb   year rows_eu27 identical_to_course_file
 ZA4056 61.0 2004 16216     TRUE
 ZA4229 62.0 2004 26807     TRUE
 ...
 ZA5689 79.3 2013 26605     TRUE

 check                                                           value
 files found                                                      16
 files identical to the course build                              16
 country-years in the committed panel                            270
 country-years rebuilt                                           270
 cells with an identical respondent count                        270
 cells with identical no-opinion counts (none, DK, other, blank) 270

Every check passed: your file is the one from which the course panel was built.
```

The respondent file then holds `r format(sum(panel$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` rows and 31 columns, the respondents of the 270 country-years.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Run the script and read the report. Then open `data_private/build_report.csv` and find the wave with the fewest respondents. It is the spring 2004 wave, fielded before the ten accession states joined; every later wave has about twenty-six and a half thousand respondents in the twenty-seven states.
:::

### 4.2 Which items form which scale {#sec-items}

`prep/02_scales_and_panel.R` is written to be read from the top and run a section at a time. It makes the measurement decisions of the course explicit one at a time, in the order in which the pipeline needs them. The published paper assigns the thirteen scored items to four scales, cosmopolitan, utilitarian, communitarian and libertarian, and the course adds the positive and the negative composite. The script states the assignment as four vectors of item names, since at this point a scale is no more than a list:

```{r}
#| label: eu-items
#| eval: false
items <- list(
  cosmo = paste0("it", c(1, 3, 5, 6, 7)),  # peace, democracy, travel, diversity, say
  util  = paste0("it", c(2, 4)),           # prosperity, social protection
  comm  = paste0("it", c(9, 12, 13, 14)),  # unemployment, identity, crime, frontiers
  lib   = paste0("it", c(10, 11))          # bureaucracy, waste of money
)
items <- c(items, list(pos = c(items$cosmo, items$util), neg = c(items$comm, items$lib)))
items13 <- c(items$pos, items$neg)
```

The euro item (`it8`) is kept in the respondent file and never scored, as in the paper. The [measurement module](measurement.qmd) tests whether the data agree with the assignment.

### 4.3 Three scoring rules {#sec-scoring}

The answers of a respondent to a set of items can become one number in more than one way, and the full menu of the course offers three: the share, which is the published rule and divides the mentions of items in the set by the total of the respondent; the count, which is the number of items in the set that were mentioned; and the per-item rate, which divides the count by the number of items in the set. The script computes all three for every scale, side by side, from the same item columns, adding a count (`c_`), a share (`s_`) and a rate (`r_`) for one scale at a time with `purrr::reduce()`:

```{r}
#| label: eu-scoring
#| eval: false
scored <- names(items) |>
  purrr::reduce(\(d, s) {
    d |>
      dplyr::mutate("c_{s}" := datawizard::row_sums(dplyr::pick(dplyr::all_of(items[[s]]))),
                    "s_{s}" := dplyr::if_else(n_all == 0, 0, .data[[paste0("c_", s)]] / n_all),
                    "r_{s}" := .data[[paste0("c_", s)]] / length(items[[s]]))
  }, .init = dplyr::mutate(respondents,
                           n_all = datawizard::row_sums(dplyr::pick(dplyr::all_of(items13)))))
```

The share is compositional, meaning that the four scales sum to one for anyone who mentioned anything. The count measures how many items were mentioned, and its four scales have no such constraint. That is why the specification menu treats the rule as a decision about what the outcome is rather than about how it is measured, and the curve of the claim keeps only the share, for the reasons that the [measurement module](measurement.qmd#sec-count) gives.

### 4.4 The respondent who named nothing {#sec-noop}

About six per cent of respondents mentioned none of the thirteen items, and a share has no denominator for them. The code of the original study drops them, since a division by a total of zero leaves them missing, while the course panel scores them zero on every scale, and the script does the same (the `if_else()` above); the curve of the claim keeps both rules. The [missing-answers module](missingness.qmd) sets out the alternatives, which are dropping them, splitting them across the scales, or imputing them. The first script keeps the "don't know", "other" and blank codes apart because the three groups are different people, and treating them alike is itself a decision.

### 4.5 From respondents to country-years {#sec-aggregate}

The course panel averages every respondent in a country-year with the same weight, which the course calls 'as interviewed'. The post-stratification weight that GESIS supplies with each file, which corrects a national sample to its population, is the other choice, and the script computes both means so that the two can be compared in the [weights module](weighting.qmd). It also records the count of respondents in each cell, which is used by a precision weight at the next stage.

```{r}
#| label: eu-aggregate
#| eval: false
cells <- scored |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("s_"), mean, .names = "m{.col}"),
    dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("s_"), \(x) stats::weighted.mean(x, w1), .names = "w{.col}"),
    dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("c_"), mean, .names = "m{.col}"),
    n_cy = dplyr::n(),
    .by = c(cntry, year)
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename_with(\(x) sub("^ms_", "m", x), dplyr::starts_with("ms_")) |>
  dplyr::rename_with(\(x) sub("^ws_", "w_m", x), dplyr::starts_with("ws_")) |>
  dplyr::rename_with(\(x) sub("^mc_", "c_m", x), dplyr::starts_with("mc_"))
```

This is the step at which the licensed microdata become an aggregate that may be shared: from here on, every row is a country-year, and the smallest mean in the panel rests on `r format(min(panel$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` respondents.

### 4.6 The macro series {#sec-merge}

The unemployment rate and the growth series join the panel by country and year. The script merges them from the file that contains every series offered by the menu, `predictor_measures.csv`, which is distributed with the course so that the merge works offline; the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-worldbank) shows the call of the `WDI` package that fetches the same World Bank indicators live. A live fetch can differ in the last decimals because the Bank revises past years, so the course records which release of each series it used. This step reads only committed files, so this page runs it and compares the result with the two columns of the panel:

```{r}
#| label: eu-merge
macro <- measures |>
  datawizard::data_filter(measure %in% c("wb_nat", "wb_growth")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("cntry", "year", "predictor", "value")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = predictor, values_from = value)

panel |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("cntry", "year", "unemp", "growth")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(macro, by = c("cntry", "year"), suffix = c("_panel", "_merged")) |>
  dplyr::summarise(rows = dplyr::n(),
                   unemp = max(abs(unemp_panel - unemp_merged)),
                   growth = max(abs(growth_panel - growth_merged)))
```

The two series agree with the panel exactly in all 270 country-years. The bailout indicator is not merged from any file. It is coded by rule from the record of assistance programmes, and the codebook states the rule.

### 4.7 Does it reproduce the panel? {#sec-reproduce}

The rebuilt panel is compared column by column with the panel distributed with the course. On the file from which the course was built, the six as-interviewed scale means, the respondent counts and the two macro series agree to machine precision, and so do the design-weighted and the count-built means in the cell file:

```
 column max_abs_difference
 mcosmo 5.551115e-17
 mutil  2.775558e-17
 mcomm  5.551115e-17
 mlib   2.775558e-17
 mpos   5.551115e-17
 mneg   5.551115e-17
 n_cy   0.000000e+00
 unemp  0.000000e+00
 growth 0.000000e+00
```

A difference of five parts in a hundred million billion is the rounding of floating-point arithmetic, not a difference in the data.

A reproducible data pipeline, in the sense used in this course, is one in which anyone with the same sixteen files and this script gets the same 270 rows, and can alter any decision above and find out what changes in the panel.

### 4.8 The panel by education band {#sec-edu}

The last section of the script builds a second panel, one row per country, year and education band, with the same six scales and the number of respondents behind each mean. It is the aggregate used in the individual-level extension of the course to ask whether unemployment narrows the gap between the high- and the low-educated. Unlike the respondent file, it can be committed and shared, because a cell mean over at least `r min(by_edu$n)` people, and in half of the cells more than `r floor(stats::median(by_edu$n))`, reveals nothing about any of them. Its `r format(nrow(by_edu), big.mark = ",")` rows are `cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy_edu.csv`, and the rebuild reproduces them to machine precision.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Change the scoring rule in section 4.3 from the share to the count for the cosmopolitan scale, re-run the aggregation and the comparison, and read the column of differences. The as-interviewed cosmopolitan mean now differs from the course panel in every cell, and the count-built column of the cell file agrees instead. Then change the no-opinion rule so that respondents who named nothing are dropped rather than scored zero, and read the respondent counts. Each is a one-line change in the script and a decision on the specification menu.
:::

## 5. Beyond these cases {#sec-beyond}

The six steps of section 1 recur in most survey work, and the three builds show them in three shapes: a stack of survey rounds that share their names, a fixed-width file read by positions and turned into events in time, and many waves aggregated into a panel. The [section of the R module on other formats](intro-r.qmd#sec-formats) has the functions for the file formats, and the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd) the routes by which the raw files arrive. Three habits from these builds apply to any project. Keep an inventory of the files that you read, with their versions and checksums, in the script itself, so that the data on which a result rests are stated where the result is computed. Check every build against a target that you did not compute, a count printed in the paper or a file that someone else built, and write the check into the script so that it runs every time. And keep the licensed and the shareable in different folders from the first day, with the ignore rule written before the first file is downloaded.
